The language remains in use as the [[liturgical language]] of the [[Georgian Orthodox Church]] and for the most part is still [[Mutual intelligibility|intelligible]]. Spoken Old Georgian gave way to what is classified as [[Middle Georgian]] in the 11th century, which in turn developed into the [[Modern Georgian]] in the 18th century. ==Periodization== Two periods are distinguished within Old Georgian: Early Old Georgian (5th to 8th centuries) and Classical Old Georgian (9th to 11th centuries). Two different dialects are represented in Early Old Georgian, known as Khanmet’i (ხანმეტი, 5th to 7th c.) and Haemet’i (ჰაემეტი, 7th and 8th c.). They are so named after the presence of a second-person subject prefix and a third-person object prefix ''kh-'' or ''h-'' in the verbal morphology where Classical Old Georgian has ''h-'', ''s-'' or zero.Tuite (2008:146). ==Texts== {{Main|Old Georgian prefix}} The corpus of Early Old Georgian texts is limited in size, consisting of a dozen inscriptions and eight manuscripts containing religious texts. The literature in Classical Old Georgian has a wider scope, including philosophical and historiographical works. ==Phoneme inventory== Old Georgian had 29 phonemic consonants and 5 phonemic vowels. The native spelling also distinguishes the semivowel ''y'', which is an allophone of the vowel ''i'' in postvocalic position. The table shows the consonants in the [[Romanization of Georgian|National Transliteration System]] (2002). This system leaves aspiration unmarked, and marks glottalization with an apostrophe. "Did s/he/it come?"). ==Morphosyntax== Old Georgian verbs are [[polysynthetic]] with [[noun incorporation]] as an active morphosyntactic process; the incorporated object always precedes the head. {{Interlinear|indent=3|abbreviations=PRV:preradical vowel|adgil-i-p’q’r{{=}}a mun, sada i-q’{{=}}o, or dğe|place-PRV-destroy{{=}}3SG.SUBJ.AOR there where PRV-be{{=}}3SG.SUBJ.AOR two days|'he laid waste there where he was for two days'}} {{Interlinear | indent = 3 | abbreviations = PVB:preverb; PRV:preradical vowel; SCV:screeve marker|vin aka s̆ina tawq'an-is-x-c{{=}}es ğ[mertma]n s̆e-i-c'q'al-e-n|Who.NOM here inside worship-GEN-3SG.OBJ-give{{=}}3PL.SUBJ God-ERG PVB-PRV-bless-SCV-NOM.PL|'May God bless whoever worships inside here [this church]' }} ==Script== {{Main|Georgian scripts}} Old Georgian was written in its own alphabetic script, known as ''[[Asomtavruli]]'' "capital letters" or ''Mrglovani'' "rounded". The alphabet is very nearly phonemic, showing an excellent "fit" between phonemes and graphemes. It is clearly modelled on the Greek alphabet, showing basically the same alphabetic order, and with letters representing non-Greek phonemes gathered at the end. Apart from letters for nearly all Georgian phonemes, the alphabet also contains three letters representing Greek phonemes not found in Georgian (''ē'', ''ü'' and ''ō''). Most individual letters seem to be entirely independent designs, with only a few based directly on their Greek counterparts (cf. Transliteration | s || t’ || ü || p || k || gh || q’ || sh || ch || ts || dz || ts’ || ch’ || kh || q || j || h || ō || |} ==Orthography== Old Georgian orthography is quite consistent, in the sense that the same word is usually written in the same way in all instances. Spelling is nearly phonemic, with almost all phonemes exclusively represented by a single letter. The exceptions are described below.This section is mainly based on Schanidse (1982:18–33). ;Vowel ''u'' The most conspicuous exception to the rule that each phoneme is written with its own letter is the vowel ''u'', which is consistently written with the [[Digraph (orthography)|digraph]] '''ႭჃ''' {{angbr|oü}}, for example '''ႮႭჃႰႨ''' {{angbr|p’oüri}} ''p’uri'' "bread". This usage was evidently adopted from Greek spelling, which writes {{IPA|/u/}} as {{angbr|ου}}. In the later Nuskhuri script, the original digraph '''ⴍⴣ''' {{angbr|oü}} merged into a single letter '''ⴓ''' {{angbr|u}} (modern Mkhedruli script '''უ'''). A matching Asomtavruli single-letter counterpart '''Ⴓ''' was then devised; this letter was not part of the original alphabet, and was not used in the Old Georgian period. ; Semivowel ''w'' The semivowel ''w'' is written in two ways, depending on its position within the word. When it occurs directly after a consonant, it is written with the digraph '''ႭჃ''' {{angbr|oü}}, for example '''ႹႭჃႤႬ''' {{angbr|choüen}} ''chwen'' "we", '''ႢႭჃႰႨႲႨ''' {{angbr|goürit’i}} ''gwrit’i'' "turtledove". The digraph '''ႭჃ''' {{angbr|oü}} thus represents both ''w'' and ''u'', without differentiation in the spelling, for example '''ႵႭჃႧႨ''' {{angbr|khoüti}} {{Transliteration|oge|khuti}} "five" vs. '''ႤႵႭჃႱႨ''' {{angbr|ekoüsi}} {{Transliteration|oge|ekwsi}} "six". In all other positions, ''w'' is written with the letter '''Ⴅ''' {{angbr|v}}, for example '''ႧႭႥႪႨ''' {{angbr|tovli}} {{Transliteration|oge|towli}} "snow", '''ႥႤႪႨ''' {{angbr|veli}} ''weli'' "field", '''ႩႠႰႠႥႨ''' {{angbr|k’aravi}} ''k’arawi'' "tent". The two spellings of {{IPA|w}} clearly represent an allophonic variation like the one described for modern Georgian,Aronson (1997:930). between {{IPA|[w]}} in postconsonantal position and {{IPA|[ʋ]}} or {{IPA|[β]}} in other positions. In modern Georgian spelling (as standardized in 1879), both {{IPA|[w]}} and {{IPA|[ʋ/β]}} are consistently written with '''ვ''' {{angbr|v}}, and spellings with '''Ⴅ''' {{angbr|v}} instead of the expected '''ႭჃ''' {{angbr|oü}} are already found in Old Georgian.Schanidse (1982:26) lists a number of words which are written with '''Ⴅ''' {{angbr|v}} instead of the expected '''ႭჃ''' {{angbr|oü}}. This seems to be an orthographical convention, as in all cited examples ''w'' is followed by a vowel and ''l'' ('''ႠႣႥႨႪႨ''' {{angbr|advili}} ''adwili'' "easy", '''ႷႥႤႪႨ''' {{angbr|q’veli}} ''q’weli'' "cheese", etc.), with just one exception ('''ႰႥႠ''' {{angbr|rva}} ''rwa'' "eight"). Romanized transcriptions of Old georgian conventionally reflect the different spellings of ''w'', for example {{Transliteration|oge|chwen}}, ''gwrit’i'', {{Transliteration|oge|tovli}}, ''veli''. ;Semivowel ''y'' The initial vowel ''i-'' of a case suffix is realized as ''y-'' after a vowel, and this allophonic ''y'' has its own letter in the alphabet, for example: {{fs interlinear|lang=oge|indent=2 |ႣႤႣႠჂ ႨႤႱႭჃჂႱႠ |⟨deday iesoüysa⟩|italics2=no |deda-y iesu-ysa|italics3=yes |mother-NOM Jesus-GEN|glossing4=yes |"the mother of Jesus"}} ;The "Greek" letters The Asomtavruli alphabet contains three letters which are not needed for the writing of native words: '''Ⴡ''' {{angbr|ē}}, '''Ⴣ''' {{angbr|ü}} and '''Ⴥ''' {{angbr|ō}}. These were added to the alphabet in order to make possible a letter-for-letter transliteration of Greek names and loanwords. They were indeed occasionally used to write the Greek vowels ''ē'' (ēta), ''ü'' (ypsilon) and ''ō'' (ōmega). As these vowels are alien to Georgian, they were replaced in actual pronunciation by ''ey'', ''wi'' and ''ow'' respectively, as can be deduced from old variant spellings, and from corresponding modern forms. For example, Greek '''Αἴγυπτος''' is written '''ႤႢჃႮႲႤ''' {{angbr|egüp’t’e}} ''egwip’t’e'' "Egypt" (cf. modern Georgian '''ეგვიპტე''' ''egvip’t’e''). In native words, the letter '''Ⴥ''' {{angbr|ō}} was mainly used to write the vocative particle, for example: {{fs interlinear|lang=oge|indent=2 |Ⴥ ႣႤႣႨႩႠႺႭ |⟨ō dedik’atso⟩|italics2=no |o dedik’atso|italics3=yes |"o woman!"}} The letters '''Ⴡ''' {{angbr|ē}} and '''Ⴣ''' {{angbr|ü}} on the other hand were frequently used in the spelling of native words, as a short-hand way of representing the sequences ''ey'' and ''wi'', for example '''ႫႤႴჁ''' {{angbr|mepē}} {{Transliteration|oge|mepey}} "king", '''ႶჃႬႭჂ''' {{angbr|ghünoy}} ''ghwinoy'' "wine". Spelling can thus vary within a paradigm, for example '''ႱႨႲႷႭჃႠჂ''' {{angbr|sit’q’oüay}} ''sit’q’wa-y'' "word" (nominative case) vs. '''ႱႨႲႷჃႱႠ''' {{angbr|sit’q’üsa}} ''sit’q’w-isa'' (genitive).Schanidse (1982:41). The sequences ''ey'' and ''wi'' could also be written out in full however, for example '''ႫႤႴႤჂ''' {{angbr|mepey}} {{Transliteration|oge|mepey}}, '''ႶႭჃႨႬႭჂ''' {{angbr|ghoüinoy}} {{Transliteration|oge|ghwinoy}} "wine" (also '''ႶჃႨႬႭჂ''' {{angbr|ghüinoy}}, a mixed spelling). ==Notes== {{notelist}} ==References== {{reflist|2}} ==Bibliography== *{{cite book | author=Aronson, Howard J. | year=1997 | chapter=Georgian phonology | editor=Alan S.
